blocks.p: Rei found the eleventh seat the way the bookseller's note told him to. Not by an address. By a hunger that was not his own, in a street that had spent thirty years learning to smell like home for people who had left theirs behind.

He went there late. He took the Saikyō line from Jūjō to Ikebukuro and changed to the Yamanote line. The train was full of people going out for the night. Two girls in matching sandals shared one pair of earphones, a wire running from one ear to the other, and nodded to the same song. A man in a crumpled shirt slept standing up, holding the strap, and woke at every station just long enough to read the sign. Three stops later the doors opened at Shin-Ōkubo. It is a small station with a narrow platform, and the crowd squeezed down the stairs and out through the ticket gates in a long beeping line of Suica cards.

Shin-Ōkubo is Tokyo's Koreatown. At midnight, in the second week of Obon, its main street was a long bright corridor of Korean signs and Korean cooking. Shops sold face masks and pop-star posters. The air was thick with grilling pork, fermented chilli and the sugary smoke of street toast. Under all of it, threading through the festival crowd the way the cold had threaded the stairwell, ran a low, steady pull. Rei recognised it at once now. It was not the pull of more, like the Hunger seat. It was the pull of back. A leaning toward something behind him. A reaching for a place that was always one country and several years away.

If he let it, the pull turned into a picture. A particular kitchen. A particular voice calling him in to eat. A particular evening light. He was fairly sure he had never lived that evening. He was homesick for it anyway, with his whole chest.

The note had named the person and the room. Park Junho, eleventh of the Thirteen. A shrine room behind a restaurant called Eomma's. Rei read the sign from across the street and understood that the name was not an accident. Eomma is the Korean word for mother.

The restaurant itself was full and loud and ordinary. Families. Drunk students. A grandmother working the grill with both hands, her sleeves pinned back. At a corner table a young man in a good suit sat alone over a bowl of instant ramyeon, the Korean instant noodles that were the cheapest thing on the menu. He ate it slowly, the way people eat when they need to feel real. Between mouthfuls he glanced at his reflection in the black window. Once he moved his lips at it, as if the glass had spoken first.

Rei felt it as he passed. Something thin and fond in the glass, very faint, fading the way a voice fades down a corridor. A dead man giving advice to a living one. He noted it, the way he noted everything that month, and kept walking.

There was a second door at the back, past the toilets. It was an old door of paper and wood that did not match the bright tiles of the rest of the place. The back was loudest there. It gathered and waited, the way water gathers at the lowest point of a floor. Through the gap Rei could see candlelight and the dull shine of a brass bowl. A man knelt in front of a small altar with his back to the door. He was holding very still, and the stillness cost him. It was the stillness of someone bracing a great weight so that it would not slide.
He spoke without turning round. His Japanese was over-careful. It was the Japanese of a man who had learned it as an adult and had never stopped feeling like a guest in it.
"You feel it from the street," he said. "Then you're not here to eat. Come in. But understand the room first."

Rei slid the door open and stepped through. The pull thickened around him like warm water. He felt it test his own walled-off places, the way every register had tested them. It found the homesickness he kept packed away with everything else. The want for a kitchen and a voice and an evening, all of it sealed off by the suppression along with the rest.

"This room makes people miss what they can't have," Park Junho said. He was still facing the altar, his shoulders set against the load. "That's all it does. It doesn't lie. It turns the longing all the way up and won't let it down again. And during Obon, with the dead so close, that is a very dangerous thing to do to people who came here because they were already missing someone."

He told Rei the rest while kneeling. To tell it standing, he would have had to leave the altar. The altar was where he kept the room from spilling out through the second door into a street full of the homesick.

"A holder doesn't end the longing," Park Junho said. "You can't. Longing isn't a want that gets the thing and stops. It's the gap itself. The distance between a person and the place they came from. That distance is real and it is permanent, and somebody has to carry it so it doesn't pull the whole street toward a door that opens the wrong way."

He looked younger than the registry made him. Rei knew from the bookseller's ledger that he was forty-one, born in Seoul, seventeen years in Tokyo. On Tuesday and Thursday evenings he taught Korean to children at the community centre two streets away. The face in the candlelight was gentle and exhausted. It was the face of a man who had left his country at twenty-four and had quietly grieved for it ever since. When the seat found him, he had turned that grief into a job.

"This room is the lowest point in the neighbourhood," he said. "Every homesick person who walks this street leaks a little. It all runs downhill. It pools here. I kneel in the pool so it doesn't rise high enough to drown anyone. That's the whole work. I am a drain with a face."

The paper door slid open behind them. A woman in her fifties came in without knocking, down the narrow stair from the rooms above the restaurant. A drumstick was still tucked through her belt. She set a cup of barley tea by Park Junho's knee and another by Rei's, and looked at Rei for a long moment with small black eyes that missed nothing.

blocks.cap: Pak Sun-ja, the mudang, at work in her shrine room

blocks.p: "Pak Sun-ja," Park Junho said, by way of introduction, without lifting his eyes from the altar. "She lives upstairs. Her shrine is behind the curtain up there. She keeps my secret, and she let me have this room when I needed a low place."

Rei had seen the name in Gin's book, on the page about the places people go when the CVD would only make things worse. The mudang in Shin-Ōkubo. She negotiates rather than banishes. Best for grief-anchored spirits. Gin's note meant that she talked to the dead instead of throwing them out.

"The dead are not gone, only unquiet," Pak Sun-ja said. Her Japanese was rough and fast. "I can ask them. Sometimes they answer. Grandmothers who followed their grandsons here. Husbands who don't know they're finished. I ask them what they want and I tell them where to go. Most of them listen." She jerked her chin at the kneeling man. "This one doesn't need asking. This one needs someone to sit in his place for an hour. I can't do it. The room knows my drum. You, it doesn't know yet."
She went out again. The door slid shut on the noise of the front room.

Rei knelt in the candlelight with the dull brass bowl between them, and he understood the plain, unglamorous truth of the eleventh seat. It was not a power. It was a posture. A man held the lowest place so that the flood had somewhere to go that was not a person. He did not go home. He could not. It was not a matter of money or papers. The seat was tied to the gap. If he closed the gap, if he really went back to the kitchen and the voice and the evening light, the lowest point would fill up, and the pool would rise up the street.

"People think the hard part is being far from home," Park Junho said. "It isn't. The hard part is that I could go. There's a flight. There's a city. There's a house with my mother still in it, getting older while I kneel here being the reason a hundred strangers don't drown in missing their own. The room knows that. The only handle the register has on me is exactly how much I want to go home."

And there it was. The crack. Rei had seen the same shape in the fourth seat and the ninth. It was the human want that the impersonal register gets its fingers into. The Fear holder had been afraid of failing. The Hunger holder had been starving for rest. This one was homesick to the bone, and he held the very seat that punished him for it. The domain was distance. It was nobody's fault. It was one of the true gaps the world is built from. But the longing to go home was his own, and it was new again every single day. It was exactly the want the room reached for. He could not stop feeling it, because he was a son whose mother was growing old in a house he still kept the lights on in, inside his head.

Park Junho turned his head and looked at Rei across the bowl. He read the pressed-down registers, the searching, the sealed homesickness. The others had looked at Rei with hunger or with hope. This one looked at him with the flat recognition of a man meeting his own condition in a stranger.
"You've got a home you can't get to either," he said quietly. "Walled off. I can feel it leaking from here. How do you kneel in this room and not go under?"
Rei asked him the question he asked all of them now. He had stopped believing in coincidence and had learned to read the handwriting.
"Has anyone been kind to you lately? Soft-voiced. Turned up around the time the kneeling got harder. Offered you the one thing you'd given up letting yourself want?"
Park Junho went still in a new way. It was not the braced stillness of the seat. It was the stillness of a man touching a bruise.

"There's a woman," he said. "She comes to the restaurant. Sits in the front. Always orders the things my mother used to make. Han-ssi, she says her name is. Three weeks ago she found her way back to this room. Nobody finds their way back to this room. Even Sun-ja has to knock. She knelt beside me and she didn't leak homesickness at all, which should have told me something. She put her hand on my shoulder and she called me aga."
His voice did something complicated on the word.

"It means baby. It's what a mother calls a small child. My mother hasn't called me that since I was six, and I have not heard it in this country in fifteen years, not since the last time I went home. She said it like she had every right to. And I knelt here and I cried, which I have not done since the seat found me."

It was not kindness. Rei had read the ledger. He knew this handwriting now. It was the patient mercy that hollowed out the seats holding up the sky. Someone had found the one thing a Longing holder could not afford to be given. The feeling of having arrived. Of being home. A mother's word in a mother's language. They had wrapped it in a soft voice, a familiar dish and a pet name no stranger should know to use.

Every time she came, she gave him a few minutes of the homecoming he had refused himself for fifteen years. And every time, the room tasted what it would be like for the gap to close, the gap it existed to keep open. She was not trying to comfort him. She was teaching the longing what arriving would feel like. She was raising the pool, one kind homecoming at a time. In the end the gap would close, the lowest point would fill, and the eleventh domain would spill up a street packed with the homesick. It would happen right beside a membrane that was already thin, during the festival, when the doors between here and the far shore are propped open for the dead to come home.
The thirteenth seat was empty. Their work needed the wall to lean. And this cruelty wore the face of a woman who called a lonely man baby.

"She's coming tonight," Park Junho said. The pull in the room surged as he said it. The candle flames leaned. "She said she'd bring me tteokguk. The soup you eat at New Year. The one that means you've grown a year older, that you've come through. She said I'd done so well. I'd been so far from home for so long. Didn't I think it was time I let myself come back."
He was gripping the edge of the altar now. His knuckles were pale.

"And I want to. God help me. I want to eat my mother's soup from a stranger's hands and let the gap close and let the pool rise and let it be someone else's turn to kneel in the cold. Fifteen years is so long. A bowl of soup is such a small thing to want. And she says it like coming home is allowed."
He looked at Rei.
"So before I let her in, tell me what you are. Because I think you might be the only one who could kneel here in my place long enough for me to want this and not do it."

The answer was not the soup. It was not the flight home. Rei had knelt in the pool long enough to see the whole trap. Park Junho could not go home, because going home would close the gap and raise the flood. He could not stay, because staying meant kneeling forever in a cold that was draining him faster than he could drain it. The woman offered him homecoming and poisoned it. The room offered him purpose and never let him arrive. It was the same sentence wearing two faces.
So Rei gave him the third thing, the one nobody had offered him in fifteen years. He took the lowest place for one hour, so that Park Junho could stand up.
"Move over," Rei said. "Show me where the floor is."

It was Obon, and all over the city the dead were coming home. Past the second door the street was a river of the living, missing the living and the gone. Rei knelt where Park Junho had knelt, in the pool at the bottom of all that leaking. He let the homesickness of a hundred strangers run downhill into his walled chest, where it could not reach all the way to the kitchen and the voice he kept sealed away. He was homesick in the right place, on purpose, so that the drain ran clean while its keeper stood.

He did not arrive anywhere. But he held the lowest point, the way he had climbed half a step ahead of the fear and walked half a step ahead of the appetite. He took the gap into the place in him that the suppression had sealed. Park Junho stood up from the altar for the first time in longer than he could bear to count. Rei did not go under. The pool did not rise. The lowest place was taken.

The old quiet voice started up under the noise of the festival. See. The wall is good. The home can't reach you. Why would you ever take it down. Rei left it at the second door with the rest of what he carried. He knelt in the cold of every stranger's missing while a man who had been a drain with a face remembered that he had legs.

Park Junho stood in the candlelight, rubbing his knees. He looked at Rei with an expression Rei had seen twice before that month and had come to dread. Recognition. Gratitude. And the terrible beginning of an idea about what Rei was for.
"I forgot you could be in the room without being the floor of it," he said, very quietly, watching Rei kneel where he had knelt.

Out past the door someone in the restaurant had started singing an old song in Korean, badly and lovingly. Pak Sun-ja's rough voice joined in from the stair. Half the front room took it up. A hundred homesick people were turning the gap into music instead of a flood.
"That's the trick, isn't it," Park Junho said, listening. "They're all missing home and none of them are drowning, because they're missing it together, out loud, instead of alone in the lowest room."

Something in him had eased that the soup could never have eased. Not the longing. The longing was distance and would always be distance. What eased was the fifteen-year cramp of a man who thought there were only two roads open to him. A flight home that would flood the street, or a floor he would kneel on until he died. Rei had not freed the eleventh seat. He had shown its holder that the lowest place could be shared, that a gap could be carried with someone else beside him. That was the one thing the soft-voiced woman's homecoming could never give him. Hers closed the gap. Rei only knelt beside it.

Han-ssi came while Park Junho was still standing. In Korean, ssi is a polite word added after a name, a little like Mr. or Ms. She was exactly as he had described her. A warm, ordinary woman in late middle age, holding a covered bowl in a cloth against its heat. The steam of the tteokguk reached the room before she did. It carried the smell of New Year, of growing older and of coming through.
She saw that he was on his feet and not on his knees. She saw, the way the soft-voiced ones always saw, that someone was in the lowest place who should not have been able to be there.

"Junho-ya," she said. The little ending on his name landed soft and exact, a mother's name for a grown son, and the worry in it did its gentle work of reaching for the want. "You're standing. You must be so tired of kneeling, aga. I brought you the soup. Sit down and eat it while it's hot, and let yourself be home. You've done enough. You've been far enough."

Rei watched him hear it. The soup. The name. The small mercy that was also a door the flood would love to learn. And Rei watched it fail to land the way it had landed before. For one hour that night, Park Junho had stood in a room he thought he could only kneel in. A man who has felt that difference cannot quite unfeel it.

She did not push. Her kind never pushed. A push would show the method, and the method only worked as long as it looked like nothing more than a mother's love for a son who had come a long way. She simply took in that tonight's homecoming would go uneaten. She adjusted with that same smooth ease. She set the bowl down on the edge of the altar, where its steam thinned and faded.
"The soup keeps," she said, mild and warm, to him and past him to Rei kneeling in the pool. "It always keeps. Everyone comes home in the end. Even him."

The even him was aimed at Rei. It was small and precise, a note being filed. The eleventh seat could be drained by someone with a wall instead of a country. The shaped thing kneeling in the lowest place was exactly the tool their work could use. Rei had come to keep a holder away from her door. He had also shown the people thinning the wall a new idea about who could hold a gap. He had shown them a stranger who could kneel in any lowest place, because the lowest place inside himself was already sealed.

On her way out she passed Pak Sun-ja at the foot of the stair. The mudang did not look up. She threw a pinch of coarse salt onto the grill coals behind Han-ssi's back. Salt is an old protection against spirits and bad luck. The coals spat, and the soft-voiced woman's step faltered for half a pace before she went out into the bright street.

When she had gone, the covered bowl cooling on the altar between them, Park Junho stood in the candlelight of the room he had knelt in for fifteen years. He listened to the singing die down in the front. He was not free. The gap was still the gap. He would kneel again before the night was out, because the seat was a sentence and Rei had not lifted it. But he was standing like a man who remembered the difference between a drain and a person.
"She'll find another," he said. "Someone newer to the gap. There's always somebody further from home than they can stand to be."

He was not wrong. Somewhere across the thin ward there was a seat for every want, and a soft voice with a soup or a bed or a name shaped to exactly that want. Rei could not kneel in every lowest place. But he had knelt in this one.

"Thank you for taking the floor," Park Junho said. It was the strangest gratitude Rei had ever been given, and the truest. What he meant was that a gap is something a person can carry standing up, beside someone else, instead of drowning in it alone.

On the way out Rei passed the corner table. The young man in the good suit had finished his ramyeon and was looking at the window again, at his own face in the black glass. He looked tired in a way that had nothing to do with the hour. For a moment the reflection seemed older than he was, and kinder, and sad. Then a group of students pushed past, and the glass was only glass. Rei did not stop. He had no hour left to give that night. But he knew the face, the way a person knows a door he will have to come back to.

Outside, the street was still bright. Rei walked back to the station through the smell of grilling meat and sweet toast. He caught one of the last Yamanote trains, its carriage half empty, a couple asleep on each other's shoulders at the far end. All the way home he could still feel the pull of back, faint now, like a hand letting go of his sleeve.
